latin: In platea, quae a Venetia<sup>1</sup> nuncupatur, mirabile visu est monumentum, quod in honorem Victoris Emmanuelis II (huius nominis secundi), regis Italorum, aedificatum est.
Ex hoc monumento, quod per gradus multos et tabulata assurgit, oculis est subiectum forum romanum, cuius plurimae sunt reliquiae.

Eminent inter omnia arcus, qui in honorem Titi<sup>2</sup>, Septimii Severi<sup>3</sup>, Constantini<sup>4</sup> imperatorum aedificati sunt, quibus imagines insculptae sunt<sup>5</sup>, quae rerum ab iis gestarum<sup>6</sup> memoriam prodeunt.
— Quam multa attento animo et diligenter lustranda sunt!
— Si a Capitolino monte prospicimus, ecce dextra Basilica Iulia<sup>7</sup>, Vestalium domus<sup>8</sup> et templum Iovis Statoris<sup>9</sup>.
Videmus deinde templum Veneri et Romae dicatum et Basilicam a Constantino imperatore exstructam.
Sinistra apparet Curia Maxima<sup>10</sup>, intra cuius parietes Cicero ille multas et luculentas orationes habuit.
Nec sunt praetereunda Rostra<sup>11</sup>, quo oratores ascendebant ut in contionibus<sup>12</sup> de re publica agerent.
Non sufficiat dies, si omnia numerare velimus*!
Exstant, ut videtis, columnae marmoreae et reliquiae templorum, quorum praecipua sunt templum Saturni, templum Castoris et Pollucis et templum Vestae.
— Displicet quod nimis multae sunt reliquiae nec otium est nobis singulatim eas videndi.
— Quod certe faciemus, cum maiore temporis spatio frui poterimus*.
english: Above the Piazza Venezia (which... is called), there is a monument astonishing to see, which was built in honour of Victor Emmanuel II (second of this name), king of Italy (of the Italians).
From this monument (which) [where one climbs] by numerous steps and [numerous landings] (rises), [stretches] before the eyes the [Roman] Forum, of which the remains are considerable.

Arches [of triumph] dominate [the whole] (among all things), which were built in honour of the emperors Titus, Septimius Severus and Constantine, and on which have been engraved sculptures which perpetuate the memory of [their exploits] (things accomplished by them).
— How many things there are to visit with an attentive mind and with care!
— If we look starting from the Capitol, here on the right is the Basilica Julia, the house of the Vestals and the temple of Jupiter Stator.
We then see the temple dedicated to Venus and to Rome, and the basilica built by the emperor Constantine.
On the left appears the Great Curia, within whose walls the famous Cicero [delivered] (numerous and) brilliant speeches.
And we must not forget the Rostra, where the orators climbed to treat of public affairs in their harangues.
A day would not be enough if we wanted to enumerate everything.
There remain, as you see, the marble columns and the ruins of the temples, of which the principal ones are the temple of Saturn, the temple of Castor and Pollux and the temple of Vesta.
— It [is a pity] (displeases) that these ruins are too numerous and that we do not have the time to see them one by one.
— That we will certainly do, when we can profit from a [little] more (great space) of time.

footnotes: Constantinus: emperor from 306 to 337. It is easy to guess that these three emperors were builders.
(In)sculpo, -is, -ere, sculpsi, sculptum, to engrave (on), to carve (in).
Gestus, -a, -um: perfect passive participle of gero, -is, -ere, gessi, gestum, to carry, to administer (gestio, execution, management).
Basilica Julia (cf. L. 94, N. 15): this basilica was begun by Julius Caesar (whence its name) and finished by Augustus.
Vestalis, -e, relating to Vesta, goddess of the hearth of whom one will speak in phrase 10. Used as a noun, designates the Vestals, priestesses of Vesta.
Jupiter Stator: Jupiter assumed different functions (here that of guardian or protector).
Curia maxima: the Curia designated either an administrative division, or a place of meeting where the Senate assembled.
Rostra, pl. of rostrum, -i, the beak (of a bird), the ram (of a vessel), the rostra were a tribune adorned with the rams of ships taken from the enemy.

Contio, -onis, f., assembly (of the people or of the soldiers), harangue (cf. L. 69, N. 10).

To finish, note the i's which in this lesson replace the j's: Huius = hujus; subiectum = subjectum; cuius = cujus; Iulia = Julia; Iovis = Jovis; maiore = majore.
comments: Campus, -i, m., the plain, and not the camp (castra, -orum). — Jugerum, -i, n., acre (28,800 square feet). — Aratrum, -i, n., the plough (cf. fr. arare and the adj. aratoire). — Semen, -inis, n., the seed. — Secale, -is, rye. — Cresco, -is, -ere, crevi, cretum, to grow; decrescere, to decrease. — Cuncti, -ae, -a, all, all together (united). — Grando, -inis, f., hail. — Gelu, -us, one of the rare neuters of the 4th declension. — Messis, -is, f., the harvest. — Seges, segetis, standing sown field, standing crop. — Falx, falcis, f. (cf. L. 90, N. 5). — Jumentum, -i, n., beast of burden (ox, horse, mule, donkey). — Stramen, -inis or stramentum, -i, n., what one spreads on the ground, from sterno, -is, -ere, stravi, stratum, to spread (cf. L. 26, P. 3). — Ligo, -onis, m., the hoe; rastrum, -i, n. (and more often rastra, -orum): sort of spade with several teeth whose diminutive rastellus gave rateau (rake). — Calleo, -es, -ere (neither pft nor supine), to have calluses (callum, the callus), to be hardened to..., gave the adjective callidus, skilful, cunning.

latin: In campo sunt agri, prata, villae.
Latifundia, ut e verbo intellegi potest, sunt lati fundi, id est magnae villae, quorum agri multa jugera complectuntur.
Agricolae aratro agros arant.
Postea semina in sulcos spargunt, et humum occa aequant.
Quid seminant? — Frumentum, hordeum, secale, et etiamnunc oryzam.
Dum seges crescit, rustici caelum saepe inspiciunt.
Nix, grando, gelu, diluvium, ventus, siccitas, uno die cunctas segetes corrumpere possunt*.
Segetes flavescunt, mox messores eas falcibus secabunt.
Frumentum in horreo coacervatur donec ad molam transferatur.
Palea variis usibus usurpatur, e.g. ad jumentorum stramentum conficiendum.
Quae sunt praecipua ferramenta rustica?
Jam aratrum, occam, falcem cognoscis; adde ligonem, palam, rastellum.
His usus rem rusticam callere potes...
Hodie documentum mihi praebere debebas, ad pontem ferriviarium quem nudius tertius vidimus pertinens.
Mihi ignosce! Hujus rei oblitus sum. Nunc tempus est otiandi. Si vis, proxima hebdomada hoc videbimus.
english: In the plain there are fields, meadows, farms.
The «latifundia», as one can understand from [the] word, are large properties, that is to say large farms whose fields [extend over] many acres (embrace).
The ploughmen plough the fields with a plough.
Then they sow the seeds in the furrows, and level the earth with a harrow.
What do they sow? — Wheat, barley, rye, and even now rice.
While the crop grows, the peasants often examine the sky.
Snow, hail, frost, flood, wind, drought can destroy the whole harvest in a single day.
The harvests are turning yellow, soon the harvesters will cut them with scythes.
The grain is piled in the loft until it is transported to the mill.
The straw serves for various uses, for example to make the litter of beasts of burden.
What are the principal tools of the peasant?
You already know the plough, the harrow, the scythe; add the hoe, the shovel, the rake.
[Using] them, you can already be strong in agriculture.
Today you were to give me a document relating to the viaduct that we saw the day before yesterday.
Forgive me! I forgot (about this thing). Now it's time to rest. If you like, we will see that next week.
